sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Sound waves (physics only) (HT only)

specStatements.text: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid.

Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate which causes the sensation of sound. The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range. This restricts the limits of human hearing.
• describe, with examples, processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids. Examples may include the effect of sound waves on the ear drum
• explain why such processes only work over a limited frequency range and the relevance of this to human hearing.
Students should know that the range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

scopeNotes.statement: Examples may include the effect of sound waves on the ear drum
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification offers the ear drum as a permitted illustration rather than a prescribed list, so what is taught here is the conversion process itself, illustrated only with the ear drum and with everyday solids that do the same job — a microphone diaphragm, a loudspeaker cone, a steel rail carrying a hammer blow. Nothing beyond 'the ear drum and other parts' is named: the ossicles, cochlea, hair cells and auditory nerve do not appear, and no item depends on nerve impulses or on how the brain interprets them. Every question is answerable from the physics of converting a wave disturbance into vibrations of a solid, and back again.

concepts.term: Sound wave travelling through a solid
concepts.definition: A sound wave passing into a solid makes the particles of that solid vibrate about their fixed positions. Each particle pushes and pulls its neighbours, so the disturbance is passed on through the material while the material itself stays where it is.
A thin membrane at the inner end of the ear canal. A sound wave arriving through the air makes it vibrate, so it converts a wave disturbance in the air into vibrations of a solid.
Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and it is these vibrations of solid parts that cause the sensation of sound.

The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works only over a limited frequency range. Outside that range the solid does not respond well enough to the pressure variations for the wave to be converted, however intense the wave is.

Because the conversion of sound waves into vibrations of solids in the ear works only over a limited frequency range, human hearing is itself restricted: the range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), one hertz being one vibration per second. One kilohertz (kHz) is 1000 Hz, so the upper limit of normal human hearing, 20 kHz, is 20 000 Hz — a thousand times the lower limit of 20 Hz.

concepts.term: Converting between sound waves and vibrations in solids
concepts.definition: The conversion works in both directions. A sound wave in air can set a solid vibrating (an ear drum, a microphone diaphragm), and a solid made to vibrate can push on the air and generate a sound wave (a loudspeaker cone, the body of a guitar).

misconceptions.question: Can a sound wave travel through a solid wall?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Sound waves can travel through solids, causing vibrations in the solid, and the vibrating solid passes the wave on.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound needs air, so a solid such as a wall or a steel rail blocks it completely; anything you hear must have reached you through the air instead.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn correctly that sound cannot travel through a vacuum and then compress 'sound needs a medium' into 'sound needs air', which makes every solid a barrier rather than a carrier.
misconceptions.correction: A medium is anything made of particles. Solids carry sound well because their particles are close together and strongly linked, which is why a hammer blow is heard clearly along a long steel rail.

misconceptions.question: What is moving when sound passes through a brick wall?
misconceptions.correct: The particles of the brick vibrate about their positions; that vibration of the solid is the wave.
misconceptions.misconception: The sound squeezes through tiny air gaps or pores between the particles of the solid, while the solid itself stays still.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sound is first met as a wave in air, so students keep air as the only thing that can really carry it and look for a route for the air to follow through the solid.
misconceptions.correction: No air path is needed. The specification states that sound waves travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid — the solid is the medium, not an obstacle with holes in it.

misconceptions.question: Why can a human not hear a 45 kHz bat call?
misconceptions.correct: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations in the ear works only over a limited frequency range, and 45 kHz lies outside it.
misconceptions.misconception: It is all about loudness — any sound can be heard if it is intense enough, and a sound you cannot hear is simply too quiet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience of turning up a volume control makes amplitude the obvious explanation for audibility, and frequency is rarely offered as a separate limit.
misconceptions.correction: The limit is a frequency limit, not an amplitude limit. Above about 20 kHz the parts of the ear cannot be driven into useful vibration, so raising the intensity does not create the sensation of sound.

misconceptions.question: How many hertz is 20 kHz?
misconceptions.correct: 20 kHz is 20 000 Hz, because one kilohertz is 1000 Hz.
misconceptions.misconception: The 'k' just means a bigger number, so 20 kHz is read as roughly 2000 Hz, or else as 200 000 Hz.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Prefixes are handled by feel rather than by value, and both limits of hearing begin with the digits '20', which invites students to guess at the scaling between them.
misconceptions.correction: kilo means x1000 every time. 20 Hz is the lower limit and 20 kHz = 20 000 Hz is the upper limit, so the two limits are a factor of a thousand apart.

misconceptions.question: What happens inside the ear when a sound wave arrives?
misconceptions.correct: The sound wave causes the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and these vibrations cause the sensation of sound.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing physically vibrates — the ear converts the sound straight into an electrical signal, and it is the brain that decides which frequencies get through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Biology lessons emphasise nerve impulses and the brain, so the mechanical step is skipped and the frequency limit is blamed on the brain rather than on the conversion.
misconceptions.correction: The mechanical step comes first and is where the limit lies: the wave must set solid parts of the ear vibrating, and that conversion only works over a limited frequency range.

misconceptions.question: Is a 45 kHz pressure wave in air a sound wave?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It is a sound wave; it simply lies outside the range that normal human hearing can detect.
misconceptions.misconception: If nobody can hear it, it is not sound — sound waves only exist between 20 Hz and 20 kHz.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The audible range is taught as 'the range of sound', so students treat a limit on human perception as a limit on the physics itself.
misconceptions.correction: 20 Hz to 20 kHz is the range of normal human hearing, not the range of sound. Ultrasound and infrasound are sound waves that the human ear cannot convert.

misconceptions.question: Can vibrations of a solid produce a sound wave?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The conversion runs both ways: a vibrating solid such as a loudspeaker cone pushes on the air and generates a sound wave.
misconceptions.misconception: The conversion only goes one way — sound waves make solids vibrate, but a vibrating solid cannot make a sound wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ear drum is met first and is stored as a one-way example, so the process is remembered as 'sound in, vibration out' rather than as a reversible conversion.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks for processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids — between, in either direction, as a loudspeaker shows.

misconceptions.question: Does human hearing have a lower frequency limit?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Normal human hearing runs from 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so there is a lower limit as well as an upper one.
misconceptions.misconception: Only very high frequencies lie outside human hearing; low frequencies can always be heard, so there is no lower limit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ultrasound and dog whistles dominate the teaching of the audible range, and very low frequencies are felt as well as heard, which blurs the lower boundary.
misconceptions.correction: The conversion in the ear fails at both ends of the range. Below 20 Hz a wave may be felt as a vibration but it does not produce the sensation of sound.

mcqs.stem: A hammer strikes one end of a long steel rail. A student with an ear pressed against the far end hears the blow. What is happening inside the steel as the sound travels along it?

options.text: Particles of the steel vibrate about their positions and pass the disturbance on
options.rationale: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid: each particle vibrates and hands the disturbance to its neighbour.

options.text: Sound slips along the tiny gaps of air trapped between the steel particles
options.rationale: Keeps air as the only real carrier of sound and looks for a route through the metal rather than accepting the metal as the medium.

options.text: Sound leaves the rail at once and reaches the ear through the air
options.rationale: 'Sound needs air' is remembered in place of 'sound needs a medium', so the solid is treated as a barrier the wave must escape.

options.text: The rail as a whole slides towards the listener as the wave passes
options.rationale: Confuses the wave with a transfer of matter; the sound transfers energy through the rail without moving the rail along.

mcqs.stem: Music from a loudspeaker in one room can be heard through a solid brick wall in the room next door. Which statement best describes the part the wall plays?

options.text: It blocks the sound entirely, so what is heard has leaked round the edges
options.rationale: Treats a solid as a barrier to sound, which cannot explain sound arriving evenly through the middle of the wall.

options.text: The brick itself vibrates and carries the sound wave to the far side
options.rationale: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid; the vibrating brick then radiates sound into the second room.

options.text: Sound seeps through the pores of trapped air inside the brick
options.rationale: Invents an air path through the solid instead of recognising the solid itself as the medium that vibrates.

options.text: It reflects the whole wave, so only an echo is heard nearby
options.rationale: Over-applies reflection: some sound is reflected at the surface, but reflection alone cannot deliver sound to the far side.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave travelling through the air arrives at a person's ear. Which statement describes how this leads to the sensation of sound?

options.text: The ear drum turns the wave straight into electricity and never moves
options.rationale: Skips the mechanical step, which is exactly where the frequency limit on human hearing comes from.

options.text: The wave passes on unchanged along the ear canal and into the brain
options.rationale: A sound wave in air cannot continue into the brain; something solid has to be set vibrating first.

options.text: The wave makes the ear drum and other parts of the ear vibrate
options.rationale: Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, which causes the sensation of sound.

options.text: The ear amplifies the wave until it is loud enough to hear
options.rationale: Makes loudness the whole story and leaves out the conversion of the wave into vibrations of a solid.

mcqs.stem: A bat call at 45 kHz is played to a class through an ultrasonic transducer at very high intensity. Nobody in the room hears anything. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The sound is far too quiet by the time that it has reached anybody's ear
options.rationale: Blames amplitude when the intensity is stated to be high; the limit on hearing is a limit on frequency.

options.text: A 45 kHz pressure wave in air is not a sound wave, so there is nothing to hear
options.rationale: Confuses the range of normal human hearing with the range over which sound waves can exist at all.

options.text: Only very high frequencies are lost, and hearing them can be trained back
options.rationale: Student holds m08 (only high frequencies fall outside hearing) and wrongly thinks such hearing can be retrained.

options.text: The ear cannot convert a wave of that frequency into vibrations
options.rationale: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range, and this restricts the limits of human hearing.

mcqs.stem: A singer's voice is picked up by a microphone and played back through a loudspeaker. Which statement correctly describes what happens at the microphone diaphragm and at the loudspeaker cone?

options.text: Both the diaphragm and the cone turn a sound wave into vibrations of a solid
options.rationale: Stores the conversion as one-way, so the loudspeaker is described backwards; a driven cone has to generate the wave.

options.text: The diaphragm vibrates the air, while the cone stops the air vibrating
options.rationale: Reverses the microphone and turns the loudspeaker into a damper; neither device works that way round.

options.text: Sound waves set the diaphragm vibrating, and the vibrating cone makes sound waves
options.rationale: The conversion runs between sound waves and vibrations in solids in both directions, which is exactly what a microphone and a loudspeaker do.

options.text: Neither part is a solid vibrating, so no conversion of the wave can occur
options.rationale: Denies that a solid part can carry the disturbance at all, which leaves the sound with no route through either device.

mcqs.stem: A drum is struck in a hall and a listener standing a few metres away in the air hears the beat. Which sequence of events describes what happens?

options.text: Air vibrates first, then the drum skin vibrates, and then the beat is heard
options.rationale: Puts the drum skin after the air, reversing the source and the medium at the very start of the chain.

options.text: The sound squeezes through tiny air gaps in the floor to get to the listener
options.rationale: A solid path can carry sound, but the listener is standing in air and the direct route is the wave through the air.

options.text: The drum skin vibrates and the sound wave itself travels to the brain
options.rationale: Leaves out the conversion at the ear drum, so nothing solid is ever set vibrating within the ear.

options.text: The skin vibrates, a sound wave crosses the air, and the ear drum vibrates
options.rationale: A vibrating solid generates the sound wave, and the wave then converts back into vibrations of a solid at the ear drum.

mcqs.stem: Explain why the process by which the ear detects sound works only over a limited frequency range, and what this means for what a person can hear.

options.text: Sound waves outside a limited band cannot be converted into vibrations of the ear's solid parts
options.rationale: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range, and this restricts the limits of human hearing.

options.text: Outside that band no sound wave exists at all, so there is simply nothing arriving at the ear to detect
options.rationale: Turns a limit on human perception into a limit on the physics; ultrasound and infrasound are still sound waves.

options.text: The brain selects the frequencies it accepts, so the ear itself passes on every sound wave arriving
options.rationale: Moves the limit from the mechanical conversion in the ear to the brain, which the specification does not support.

options.text: The quietest sounds go first, so the range narrows whenever the wave becomes less intense
options.rationale: Substitutes an amplitude limit for a frequency limit; the boundary of human hearing is set by frequency.

mcqs.stem: What is the range of normal human hearing?

options.text: from 20 Hz to 200 kHz
options.rationale: Keeps the right digits but scales the upper limit up by a further factor of ten.

options.text: from 20 Hz to 20 kHz
options.rationale: Students should know that the range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

options.text: from 2 Hz to 20 000 Hz
options.rationale: Pushes the lower limit down by a factor of ten, treating the low end as effectively open.

options.text: from 20 Hz up to 2000 Hz
options.rationale: Misreads the lower limit by a factor of ten while getting the upper limit right.
